title: CapEx vs OpEx
subtitle: Capital spending vs operating expense - different effects on the financials
openingQuestion: Buying 10 billion of machinery: expense it all this year, or depreciate it over time?
openingOptions: Depends entirely on the accountant's own personal preference here
Depreciate it over its useful life - this is CapEx, not OpEx
Record it as a bank loan
explanation: The line between capital spending and operating spending sits on whether the spend serves many years or is used up within the period. Capital spending goes onto the balance sheet and is spread out as depreciation; operating spending goes straight onto the income statement. The consequence worth remembering: both reduce cash the same way, but only one reduces profit immediately - which is why capitalizing aggressively is a familiar way to make profit look prettier than reality.

diagram.label: Does this spend serve many years, or get used up within the period?
Many years: record as an asset, depreciate gradually
Within the period: expense it straight away
Both reduce free cash flow, but only one reduces profit right away

realWorldExample.company: Netflix: shifting from content CapEx to operating expense
realWorldExample.description: Netflix spends tens of billions of dollars a year producing original content - part of which is capitalized as an asset (content assets) and depreciated over time, significantly affecting how investors read and compare Netflix's free cash flow (FCF) against traditional media companies.

quiz.question: Why does FCF usually differ from Net Income?
options: Due to accounting errors when preparing statements, so the two never match
Due to tax being calculated in a fundamentally different way between the two metrics entirely
CapEx and changes in working capital don't pass through the P&L but affect real cash
Because dividends paid to shareholders are deducted from FCF but not from profit
quiz.explanation: FCF = Net Income + D&A − CapEx − ΔWC. D&A isn't real cash (added back). CapEx is real cash but doesn't pass through the P&L immediately (subtracted out). Changes in working capital affect cash but don't pass through the income statement. That's why FCF ≠ Net Income.

quiz.question: Why does correctly distinguishing CapEx from OpEx matter when comparing Free Cash Flow between two companies in the same industry?
options: It doesn't matter - looking at Net Income alone is enough to compare the two
Only tech companies need to distinguish CapEx from OpEx in their reporting
CapEx and OpEx have exactly identical financial effects, so there's no need to separate them at all
Because different capitalization policies mean heavier capitalizing makes Net Income look prettier
quiz.explanation: A capitalization policy (like Netflix capitalizing content production costs) can make Net Income look 'prettier' than reality in the short run, but the cash has actually already gone out the moment CapEx occurs - which is why sharp investors always track FCF alongside Net Income for a fuller picture.

quiz.question: Buying 10 billion in machinery, depreciated over 5 years. How does the first year affect profit and cash?
options: Profit falls by 10 billion but cash only falls by 2 billion
Both profit and cash fall by exactly 10 billion
Both fall by 2 billion, with the rest counted in following years
Profit falls by 2 billion but cash falls by the full 10 billion
quiz.explanation: CapEx pays out cash once but enters expense gradually through depreciation. This is exactly why a business investing heavily can report a pretty profit while its cash flow is negative.

quiz.question: Why does switching from buying servers to renting cloud computing improve the ROA metric?
options: Because net profit rises thanks to cost savings
Because assets on the balance sheet shrink significantly
Because rental costs are tax-deductible while depreciation is not
Because revenue rises thanks to more stable operating infrastructure
quiz.explanation: Turning CapEx into OpEx shrinks the denominator of ROA. The ratio looks prettier while the actual business capability hasn't changed - this is why you have to read carefully when comparing ROA between two companies with different infrastructure models.

quiz.question: Why is FCF usually lower than net profit at an expanding company?
options: Because interest expense is deducted twice in the FCF formula
Because depreciation is added back into cash flow, making FCF smaller than reported profit
Because CapEx is deducted directly from FCF but hasn't hit profit yet
Because tax is calculated on FCF instead of on net profit
quiz.explanation: FCF = Profit + Depreciation − CapEx − ΔWorking Capital. An expanding company has CapEx far larger than depreciation, so FCF drops below profit - and that is real cash that has actually gone out.

practicePrompt.question: A company spends 300 million buying a new server (to be used for 5 years), and 50 million paying monthly electricity and internet bills for its office. Are these two spends classified as CapEx or OpEx, and how do they affect the P&L differently?
options: The server is CapEx, depreciated 60 million a year; electricity is OpEx, expensed in the period
Both spends are CapEx because both are costs necessary for the company to operate day to day
Both spends are OpEx because both are paid in cash immediately
Classifying something as CapEx or OpEx has no effect at all on how it's recorded in the financial statements
practicePrompt.explanation: CapEx: a long-term asset, depreciated gradually over many years (like a 300-million server split over 5 years). OpEx: day-to-day operating expense, expensed in full to the P&L immediately in the period it's incurred (like electricity, internet) - distinguishing between the two directly affects the profit reported each period.

summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.

application.title: Classify this month's spending
application.message: Open up last month's spending and split it into: personal CapEx (buying a laptop, investing in a long-term course) and OpEx (food, utilities, daily entertainment).
application.secondary: This way of looking helps you assess which spending creates lasting value and which merely sustains daily life.

sections.text: CapEx and OpEx are two completely different ways of spending financially, even though they can sometimes look similar on the surface - telling the two apart correctly is the key to understanding why Free Cash Flow is often so different from Net Income.
The basic difference between CapEx and OpEx

CapEx (Capital Expenditure) is spending to buy long-term assets - machinery, real estate, large-scale software - recorded on the Balance Sheet and depreciated gradually over many years, not immediately affecting profit. OpEx (Operating Expense) is day-to-day operating expense - salaries, electricity, marketing - recorded straight onto the P&L in the period it's incurred. CapEx affects free cash flow (FCF) far more strongly than it affects Net Income.
Why FCF often looks very different from Net Income

FCF = Net Income + D&A − CapEx − ΔWorking Capital. D&A (depreciation) isn't real cash, so it's added back. CapEx is real cash spent but doesn't pass through the P&L right away, so it's subtracted out. Changes in working capital affect cash but don't pass through the income statement. Different capitalization policies between companies - for example Netflix capitalizing a large portion of its original content production costs into assets (content assets) and depreciating them gradually - can make Net Income 'look prettier' than reality in the short run, but the cash has really already been spent the moment CapEx occurs.

items: CapEx: long-term assets, depreciated gradually, hits FCF immediately but hits Net Income only slowly over many years
OpEx: day-to-day expense, recognized straight onto the P&L in the period it's incurred
Comparing FCF between companies in the same industry is more accurate than comparing Net Income, because capitalization policies can differ
Sharp investors always track FCF alongside Net Income for a fuller picture

lines: Net Income can be made 'pretty' by accounting - FCF shows where the actual cash went.
